title: Starcloud raises $250 million for orbital data centers amid constrained launch options
summary: Starcloud, a startup developing AI inference satellites, has secured a $250 million funding extension, valuing the company at $2.3 billion. The capital will expand manufacturing and advance its orbital data center spacecraft, Starcloud-3, targeting deployment via SpaceX’s Starship. The company faces challenges due to limited launch capacity, with SpaceX phasing out Falcon 9 by 2028 and competitors like Blue Origin and ULA still scaling up. Starcloud plans to launch two 8 kW compute satellites in 2027 for orbital AI tasks, primarily for U.S. government clients. The funding round included investments from Nvidia and Cisco, with Nvidia collaborating on a space-optimized GPU. Starcloud aims to leverage Starship’s cost reductions to compete with terrestrial data centers.
key_points: Starcloud raised $250M in a funding extension, valuing the company at $2.3B, led by Manhattan West Ventures with participation from Nvidia and Cisco.
The funds will expand manufacturing and accelerate development of Starcloud-3, an orbital data center spacecraft intended for SpaceX’s Starship.
Launch capacity is a major constraint; SpaceX’s Falcon 9 is set to retire by 2028, and alternatives like Blue Origin’s New Glenn and ULA’s Vulcan are not yet fully operational.
Starcloud plans to launch two 8 kW AI inference satellites (Starcloud-2) in 2027 via rideshare flights, targeting U.S. government contracts.
The company is collaborating with Nvidia to develop a space-optimized GPU, the Vera Rubin Space-1, leveraging data from its existing orbital H100 GPU.
Starcloud’s long-term strategy relies on Starship’s cost efficiency to enable competitive orbital data centers, though delays in Starship’s reusability pose risks.
